title.text: Capstone: five builds from first principles, from linear regression to attention

objects.text: Can five small builds, written from first principles, reproduce the core of what runs inside modern AI?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 18 of 18  |  Capstone
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to the last session. For seventeen sessions you collected tools: vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, gradients, probability, likelihood, entropy. Today we use them. In one session you build linear regression, logistic regression, PCA, a small neural network and attention from first principles. The question is whether such small builds contain the core of modern AI.

The question for today is this: Can five small builds, written from first principles, reproduce the core of what runs inside modern AI? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Build linear regression (normal equation and gradient descent) and logistic regression (gradient descent) with numpy
Build PCA from the covariance eigen-decomposition and a 2-4-1 neural network with backpropagation
Build scaled dot-product attention for three tokens, and pass the automatic checks of the capstone

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can build five things from first principles. Linear regression, with the normal equation and with gradient descent. Logistic regression, with gradient descent. PCA, from the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix. A small neural network, two inputs, four hidden units and one output, with backpropagation.

And scaled dot-product attention for three tokens. In the notebook your student ID generates your own data, your functions are checked automatically on it, and each check names the build it belongs to.

title.text: Your two hours: a guided tour, then the capstone

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: The tour first. Then the individual capstone, graded in the notebook. Then AI.

slides.notes:
Today is the last session. Ten minutes of recall from Session 17. Thirty-five minutes of guided tour of the five builds, with the maths of each on a formula slide and a hand example. A ten minute break. Then forty-five minutes of capstone. The graded capstone is the notebook, which you complete on your own with your own data.

The spreadsheet is a guided practice version. We finish with where this appears in AI, what to learn next, and saving your work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  How are cross-entropy, entropy and KL divergence related?
2.  What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
3.  What does a perplexity of 5 mean?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 17. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. How are cross-entropy, entropy and KL divergence related? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Cross-entropy = entropy + KL divergence. The entropy is fixed by the data, so lowering the cross-entropy lowers the KL divergence.

Question two. What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The prediction minus the target: p - y.

Question three. What does a perplexity of 5 mean? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. The model is as unsure as if it chose among about five equally likely words at each step.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 17

rows.text: How are cross-entropy, entropy and KL divergence related?
Cross-entropy = entropy + KL divergence. The entropy is fixed by the data, so lowering the cross-entropy lowers the KL divergence.
What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
The prediction minus the target: p - y.
What does a perplexity of 5 mean?
The model is as unsure as if it chose among about five equally likely words at each step.

objects.text: All three come back today: p - y trains the network, and the softmax is inside attention.

slides.notes:
Here are the short answers. Cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL divergence, and because the entropy is fixed by the data, lowering the cross-entropy lowers the KL. The gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits is the prediction minus the target. And a perplexity of five means the model is as unsure as if it chose among about five equally likely words.

Today the second answer trains our network, and the softmax appears inside attention. Which of the three would you like to hear again?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The direct formula w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y that gives the least squares weights.
A direction of largest spread in the data: an eigenvector of the covariance matrix.
The chain rule applied backwards through a network to get the gradient of the loss for every weight.
The three vectors each token makes in attention: what it looks for, what it offers and what it passes on.
Each token takes a weighted average of the value vectors, with weights from softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)).

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Normal equation. The direct formula w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y that gives the least squares weights.

Principal component. A direction of largest spread in the data: an eigenvector of the covariance matrix.

Backpropagation. The chain rule applied backwards through a network to get the gradient of the loss for every weight.

Query, key, value. The three vectors each token makes in attention: what it looks for, what it offers and what it passes on.

Attention. Each token takes a weighted average of the value vectors, with weights from softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)).

title.text:
Five builds, and each one uses
mathematics you already know

objects.alt: Five builds, and each one uses mathematics you already know

objects.text: Illustrative data. Each build is about ten lines of numpy.

slides.notes:
This is the plan for today in one picture. Linear regression uses what we learned about linear systems and least squares. Logistic regression uses gradient descent and the cross-entropy loss. PCA uses the covariance matrix and its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The neural network uses the chain rule, which is backpropagation.

And attention uses matrix multiplication, dot products and the softmax. Each build is about ten lines of numpy, and all of the data are made up to show the arithmetic. Which of the five do you expect to be hardest?

objects.text: Q = X Wq, K = X Wk and V = X Wv give three rows of two numbers each.

title.text:
Build 1: linear regression has a
direct solution and an iterative one

objects.alt: Build 1: linear regression has a direct solution and an iterative one

rows.text: The design matrix: a column of ones, then x.
The weights: intercept w0 and slope w1.

objects.text: Same weights from both. MSE 0.0213. 7 hours (beyond the data) predicts 7.98 kWh.

slides.notes:
Build one is linear regression. The model predicts X times w, where X has a column of ones so that w zero is the intercept. The normal equation solves the least squares problem in one line: w equals the inverse of X transpose X, times X transpose y.

Gradient descent reaches the same answer by small steps, using the gradient two over n times X transpose times the residual. For our six illustrative points both give an intercept of 1.12 and a slope of 0.98. The mean squared error is 0.0213. Seven hours of use is outside the data, which stops at six, so that prediction of 7.98 kilowatt-hours is an extrapolation.

Why does the column of ones matter?

title.text: Build 1 in a picture: the fitted line and its residuals

objects.alt: Build 1 in a picture: the fitted line and its residuals

objects.text: The line is y-hat = 1.12 + 0.98 x. The red segments are the residuals.

runs.text: Illustrative data: x = 1 to 6 hours, y = 2.2, 2.9, 4.1, 5.2, 5.8, 7.1 kWh.
The normal equation and gradient descent give the same line.

slides.notes:
Here is build one as a picture. Six points, and the least squares line with intercept 1.12 and slope 0.98. The red segments are the residuals, the gaps between the points and the line. Least squares chooses the line that makes the sum of their squares as small as possible.

In Session 16 you saw that this is also maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise. The data are illustrative. Which point has the largest residual?

title.text:
Build 2: logistic regression is a sigmoid on
a linear score, trained by gradient descent

objects.alt: Build 2: logistic regression is a sigmoid on a linear score, trained by gradient descent

rows.text: The prediction minus the target, as in Session 17.

objects.text: After 5 steps: w = (-0.0509, 0.1494), loss 0.623. Data: 8 students (see the data slide).

slides.notes:
Build two is logistic regression. The model passes a linear score through the sigmoid, so the output is a probability between zero and one. The loss is the binary cross-entropy from Session 16. Its gradient is wonderfully simple, and you already derived it in Session 17: the average of the prediction minus the target, times the inputs.

Starting from zero weights every probability is one half and the loss is 0.693. After five steps with a learning rate of 0.1 the weights are -0.0509 and 0.1494, and the loss has fallen to 0.623. The data are eight illustrative students: hours of study and pass or fail.

title.text:
Build 2 by hand: the loss falls at every
one of the first five gradient steps

objects.text: Learning rate 0.1. Step 0 is the start. The workbook has the same table.

slides.notes:
Here are the first five gradient steps. Step zero is the start, with both weights at zero and a loss of 0.6931. At step one the intercept stays at zero, because half the students passed and the average of p minus y for the intercept is zero, but the slope moves up.

The loss falls at every step, to 0.6232 after five. In the lab you let it run for five thousand steps, and in the workbook you fill this same table with formulas. What would happen to the table if the learning rate were 2?

title.text:
Build 3: PCA finds the direction
of largest spread in the data

objects.alt: Build 3: PCA finds the direction of largest spread in the data

objects.text: The red line is the first principal component. It holds 96.3 percent of the variance.

runs.text: Eigenvalues of the covariance matrix: 1.156 and 0.044.
First component: (0.678, 0.735).

slides.notes:
Build three is PCA, principal component analysis. Ten illustrative points in two dimensions. The two columns rise together, so the spread is mostly along one diagonal direction, the red line. That direction is the first principal component. The covariance matrix has two eigenvalues, 1.156 and 0.044, so the first component holds 96.3 percent of the total variance.

If we keep only the position of each point along that line, one number instead of two, we lose very little. Why does the spread across the line matter less?

title.text:
PCA as formulas: centre, form the
covariance, find its eigenvectors, project

objects.alt: PCA as formulas: centre, form the covariance, find its eigenvectors, project

rows.text: The data with each column centred on its mean.
An eigenvalue: the variance along its eigenvector.
The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue: the first component.

objects.text: Libraries divide by n - 1: eigenvalues 1.284 and 0.049, the same 96.3 percent share.

slides.notes:
Here is PCA as formulas. First centre each column on its mean. Then the covariance matrix is X c transpose times X c, divided by n, the convention of this course. Its eigenvectors are the principal components, and each eigenvalue is the variance along its eigenvector. For our data the largest eigenvalue is 1.156, with eigenvector 0.678 and 0.735.

The score of a point is its centred row times that eigenvector. Many libraries divide by n minus one instead. The eigenvalues are then a little larger, but the share of variance and the eigenvectors are the same. The singular value decomposition of the centred data gives the same eigenvectors.

title.text:
Build 4: a 2-4-1 network has two layers
of weights, and the error flows back

objects.alt: Build 4: a 2-4-1 network has two layers of weights, and the error flows back

objects.text: Two inputs, four hidden units, one output. The task is XOR: 1 when exactly one input is 1.

runs.text: Forward: h = tanh(W1 x + b1), then p = sigmoid(W2 h + b2). Loss: binary cross-entropy.
Backward: the chain rule passes the error signal back, layer by layer.

slides.notes:
Build four is a small neural network, two inputs, four hidden units and one output. The task is XOR, answer one when exactly one of the inputs is one. A straight line cannot solve XOR, which is why we need the hidden layer. The forward pass computes the hidden activations with tanh, then the output probability with a sigmoid.

The backward pass is backpropagation, the chain rule applied from the output back to the first layer. We use the binary cross-entropy loss, so the first backward quantity is the familiar p minus y. Why does XOR need a hidden layer?

title.text:
Backpropagation for the 2-4-1
network, in matrix algebra

objects.alt: Backpropagation for the 2-4-1 network, in matrix algebra

rows.text: The error signal at the output. For a sigmoid with binary cross-entropy it is p - y.
The error signal arriving at each hidden unit.
The slope of tanh at each hidden unit (chain rule).

objects.text: Update with learning rate eta: each weight matrix and bias becomes W - eta × its gradient.

slides.notes:
Here is backpropagation in matrix algebra. The forward pass and the loss are on top, the binary cross-entropy. Below, the first backward line says the error signal at the output, delta, is p minus y, as in Session 17. That holds for a sigmoid output with this loss.

The gradient for the second weight matrix is delta times the hidden activations, and the gradient for its bias is delta. The error signal then flows back through the second matrix and is multiplied entry by entry by one minus h squared, the slope of tanh. That gives delta h at the hidden layer, and the gradient for the first weight matrix is delta h times the input.

Each weight matrix and bias is then updated by subtracting the learning rate times its gradient.

title.text:
By hand: one forward and one backward
step for the input (1, 2) with target 1

objects.text: One illustrative example (not an XOR row), from the starting weights on the data slide. The notebook trains on many rows and averages their gradients.
Forward
Loss
Backward

slides.notes:
Let us put numbers in. The input is one and two, the target is one. With the starting weights on the data slide the four hidden activations are -0.100, 0.947, 0.197 and -0.935. The output probability is 0.3888, so the loss is 0.9446. The error signal delta is p minus y, -0.6112.

The gradient for the output weights is delta times h. With a learning rate of 0.5 the first output weight moves from 0.3 to 0.270. The first row of the gradient of W1 is -0.182 and -0.363, and the second is twice the first because the second input is 2.

The workbook has this exact example in cells. Which sign tells you the weight should go up?

title.text:
After 5,000 gradient steps the toy
network solves XOR (guided example)

objects.text: The loss falls from 0.706 to 0.0008. Learning rate 0.5.

slides.notes:
Here is what training does. Before training all four outputs are close to one half, between 0.38 and 0.53, and the loss is 0.706. After five thousand steps of gradient descent the outputs are near zero for the first and last inputs and near one for the middle two, and the loss is 0.0008.

The network has learned XOR, which no single straight line can do. In the graded notebook the checks compare your backward function with a numeric gradient, on your own data.

title.text:
Build 5: attention gives every token a
weighted average of the value vectors

objects.alt: Build 5: attention gives every token a weighted average of the value vectors

objects.text: Each row of weights adds to 1. The output is the weights times the value vectors.

slides.notes:
Build five is attention, the core step inside the transformer. Each token asks a question, a query, and every token offers a key. The score between a query and a key says how much that token should read from that one. The grid shows the attention weights after a softmax along each row, so each row adds to one.

Darker gold means a larger weight. Token three, in the last row, reads 31 percent from token one, 7 from token two and 62 from itself. On the right, the output is that weighted average of the value vectors. The numbers are made up to show the arithmetic.

title.text: Attention as a formula: every symbol named

objects.alt: Attention as a formula: every symbol named

rows.text: One row per token: its embedding.
Weight matrices that make queries, keys and values.
Queries (what a token looks for), keys (what it offers), values (what it passes on).
The length of a key vector.
Applied along each row, so each row adds to 1.

objects.text: Vaswani et al. (2017): large dot products saturate the softmax, so its gradient is tiny.

slides.notes:
Here is the formula for scaled dot-product attention, as published by Vaswani and colleagues in 2017. Each token embedding in X is multiplied by three weight matrices to give queries, keys and values. Q times K transpose gives a score for every pair of tokens. We divide by the square root of d k, the length of a key vector, then apply a softmax along each row, so each row of weights adds to one.

Finally the weights multiply V. The published reason for the square root is that for large d k the dot products grow large and push the softmax into a saturated region, where almost all the weight goes to one token and the gradient is tiny. A simulation in the following picture shows the size of the scores.

title.text:
Why divide by the square root of d: dot products
of long vectors grow, and the softmax saturates

objects.alt: Why divide by the square root of d: dot products of long vectors grow, and the softmax saturates

objects.text: If the entries of q and k are independent with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, then q . k has mean 0 and standard deviation sqrt(d).

runs.text: Large scores make the softmax saturate: almost all the weight goes to one token (nearly one-hot), and the gradient is tiny.
Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the standard deviation near 1. The notebook simulates 2,000 pairs.

slides.notes:
Why divide by the square root of d?

Take two random vectors of length 64, whose entries are independent with mean zero and standard deviation one. Their dot product is a sum of 64 terms, so its standard deviation is about the square root of 64, which is 8. In a simulation of two thousand pairs I get 8.0.

Scores of that size would make the softmax saturate, nearly one-hot, and in that region its gradient is tiny, so training would be slow. Dividing by the square root of d brings the standard deviation back to about one. This is the reason given in the original paper. You check the simulation in the notebook.

title.text:
By hand: scaled scores, weights
and output for three tokens (d = 2)

objects.text: Illustrative. Scores = Q K^T / sqrt(2). Weights = softmax of each row. Output = weights times V.

slides.notes:
Here are the numbers. The scaled scores for token one are 0.707, 0.000 and 0.707. The softmax of that row gives the weights 0.401, 0.198 and 0.401, which add to one. Multiplying the weights by the three value vectors gives the output for token one, 0.802 and 1.198.

Token three has the largest score for itself, 2.828, so it gives itself the largest weight, 0.620. In the workbook the softmax is built in cells with the stable trick of subtracting the row maximum.

title.text: Three slips that the capstone checks will catch

objects.text: The slip

runs.text: No column of ones, so no intercept.
PCA without centring the data first.
Softmax along the wrong axis, or no sqrt(d).

objects.text: The fix

runs.text: Add the column of ones to X.
Subtract each column mean first.
Softmax along each row, then divide scores by sqrt(d_k).

objects.text: Each check names its build, so read the name first.

slides.notes:
Here are three slips that the checks will catch. In linear regression, forgetting the column of ones means there is no intercept. In PCA, forgetting to centre the data means the covariance is wrong. In attention, applying the softmax down the columns gives rows of weights that do not add to one, and forgetting the square root of d changes every weight.

When a check fails, its name tells you which build to look at. Which of these would you have made?

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: attention is the core
step of every layer of a published transformer

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: attention is the core step of every layer of a published transformer

objects.text: Published research describes transformer language models as many repeated layers of attention and feed-forward steps.

runs.text: Your Build 5 is the published attention formula (Vaswani et al., 2017).
Closed products do not publish their designs. Open models such as Llama use the same core formula plus a causal mask, and other changes.

slides.notes:
Here is where the capstone appears in real systems, as published research describes transformer language models. Text becomes tokens and embeddings. Then come many repeated layers. Each layer has an attention step, which is the core of your build five, and a feed-forward step, which is matrix multiplications with a nonlinearity.

At the top a softmax gives next-token probabilities and training minimises the cross-entropy. Real models use many tokens, many attention heads and many layers. Open models such as Llama use the same core formula with a causal mask, so a token cannot read later tokens, and other changes.

The designs of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are not published, so I describe only the published framework.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: the
five builds in published models

rows.text: Every layer multiplies by a weight matrix: a linear map. Its weights are learned by gradient descent, a different method from least squares.
The last step of a classifier is a softmax of linear scores (softmax regression, the many-class version), trained with cross-entropy.
Used to inspect and compress embeddings. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) learns a low-rank update to a weight matrix: the same low-rank idea that makes the first principal components useful.
Backpropagation runs in every training step of published models.
The core step of the transformer, repeated in every layer.

objects.text: Phrased as published research describes. No claim about the internals of any closed product.

slides.notes:
Here is each build and where its idea appears. Every layer of a language model multiplies by a weight matrix, a linear map like build one, though its weights are learned by gradient descent, a different method from least squares. The last step of a classifier is a softmax of linear scores, which is softmax regression, the many-class version of build two, trained with cross-entropy.

PCA is a way to inspect and compress embeddings, and LoRA learns a low-rank update to a weight matrix, the same low-rank idea that makes the first principal components useful. Backpropagation runs in every training step. Attention is the core step of the transformer. I phrase all of this as published research describes it, with no claim about closed products.

Exit check: three questions
and their short answers

rows.text: What does each row of the attention weights add up to, and why?
To 1, because a softmax is applied along each row.
Why is the attention score divided by the square root of d_k?
Large dot products make the softmax saturate: almost all the weight goes to one token and the gradient is tiny. The scaling keeps the standard deviation near 1.
In PCA, which eigenvector is the first principal component?
The one with the largest eigenvalue, the direction of largest variance.
